title: Peripheral Blood Film Interpretation
subject: Medicine
summary: A peripheral blood film (blood smear) reveals the morphology of red cells, white cells and platelets, guiding diagnosis of anaemia, infection and haematologic disease. In low‑resource settings it often substitutes for automated counters and is essential for malaria, sickle‑cell and haemolysis work‑up.

sections.p: A peripheral blood film is a thin, stained layer of blood examined under a microscope to assess cell size, shape, colour and inclusions.
b: Provides qualitative data not captured by automated counters
Can be performed with basic laboratory equipment (microscope, Wright‑Giemsa stain)

sections.p: Severity is inferred from the proportion of abnormal cells and associated haemoglobin/haematocrit values; no formal staging system exists, but clinicians grade anaemia (mild, moderate, severe) using WHO cut‑offs.
b: Hb < 8 g/dL = severe anaemia (urgent transfusion if symptomatic)
Hb 8‑10 g/dL = moderate; monitor for cardiac stress

sections.p: Morphology points to a limited differential; in East Africa the most common patterns are:
b: Microcytic hypochromic cells → iron deficiency, chronic malaria, hookworm
Target cells → thalassaemia or haemoglobinopathies
Sickle cells → sickle‑cell disease or trait
Schistocytes → severe malaria, disseminated intravascular coagulation, mechanical valve hemolysis
Trophozoites/parasites → Plasmodium falciparum or vivax infection

sections.p: Patients present with symptoms dictated by the underlying disorder: fatigue, pallor, jaundice, fever, splenomegaly or acute collapse.
b: Iron‑deficiency anaemia – fatigue, pica, koilonychia
Severe malaria – high fever, rigors, dark urine, splenomegaly
Sickle‑cell crisis – vaso‑occlusive pain, hemoglobin drop

t.b: What cell morphology is present and what does it suggest?
What are the quantitative indices (Hb, MCV, WBC, platelets)?
Is malaria present when film is unavailable or equivocal?
Is iron deficiency the cause of microcytosis?
Is a haemoglobinopathy responsible for target or sickle cells?

sections.p: Certain film findings herald life‑threatening states.
b: Schistocytes > 1 % with falling Hb → microangiopathic haemolysis, urgent plasma exchange if TTP suspected
Heavy parasitaemia (> 5 % of RBCs) → severe malaria, requires IV artesunate and ICU care
Blast cells > 20 % → acute leukaemia, urgent referral for chemotherapy

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; supportive care follows.
b: Sickle‑cell crisis – analgesia, hydration, oxygen; avoid NSAIDs if renal impairment.
Autoimmune haemolysis – steroids (prednisone) if Coombs positive; not indicated for parasite‑related hemolysis.

sections.p: Repeat film after treatment to confirm resolution and monitor for chronic disease.
b: Iron therapy – re‑check Hb after 4 weeks; continue 3 months after normalisation.
Malaria – educate on insecticide‑treated nets, intermittent preventive therapy in pregnancy.
Sickle‑cell – vaccinate against encapsulated organisms, consider hydroxyurea for frequent crises.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic similar film appearances.
b: Thalassaemia vs iron deficiency – both microcytic; target cells point to thalassaemia, low ferritin to iron deficiency.
G6PD deficiency hemolysis vs malaria – both cause schistocytes; history of drug exposure and negative parasites favor G6PD.

sections.p: Pitfalls in interpreting a blood film.
b: Early malaria may show few parasites; a negative film does not exclude infection – use RDT.
Mild iron deficiency can appear normocytic; rely on ferritin if film is equivocal.
Artifact from poor smear technique can mimic schistocytes – repeat slide if doubtful.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid Hb fall > 2 g/dL in 24 h

faq.q: Can a blood film replace a full blood count?
faq.a: It provides qualitative clues but cannot give exact Hb or platelet numbers; use both when possible.

faq.q: Why is malaria still diagnosed on film when RDTs exist?
faq.a: Film quantifies parasite density, guides severity assessment, and detects mixed species.
Hereditary spherocytosis or immune hemolysis; a negative Coombs test favors hereditary form.

exam: A 6‑year‑old with pallor and pica has a microcytic film; which test confirms iron deficiency and why? — Serum ferritin; low ferritin confirms depleted stores, guiding iron therapy.

A patient from a malaria‑endemic area presents with fever and a film showing 6 % parasitized RBCs; what is the next immediate step? — Start IV artesunate; high parasitaemia defines severe malaria requiring urgent treatment.

Your film shows numerous schistocytes in a patient with jaundice and renal failure; what life‑threatening condition must you consider? — Thrombotic microangiopathy (e.g., TTP); requires plasma exchange and urgent specialist referral.

A smear reveals sickle cells and target cells; how do you differentiate sickle‑cell disease from trait? — Frequency of sickle cells > 30 % and clinical crises suggest disease; trait shows < 30 % and is usually asymptomatic.

In a patient with microcytic hypochromic cells and a history of chronic hookworm infection, what is the first‑line management? — Oral iron supplementation plus anti‑helminthic therapy; treats both cause and deficiency.
A film shows blasts comprising 30 % of nucleated cells; what is the most appropriate next investigation? — Bone‑marrow aspirate for classification; confirms acute leukaemia and informs chemotherapy.

Why might a peripheral smear be normal in early severe malaria, and what alternative test should you order? — Parasitaemia may be below detection threshold; order a malaria rapid diagnostic test (RDT).

A patient on penicillin develops spherocytes; Coombs test is negative. What is the likely diagnosis and management? — Hereditary spherocytosis; manage with folic acid and consider splenectomy if severe.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Collect a focused history and perform a systematic exam to identify red flags and guide investigations.
b: History: ask about fatigue, pallor, dyspnoea, chest pain, fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, recent infections, malaria exposure, sickle pain crises, bleeding, drug use, alcohol, pregnancy, HIV status, TB contact, malnutrition.

History: inquire about dietary iron intake, pica, menstrual history, chronic diarrhoea, hookworm exposure, transfusion history, splenectomy, hereditary haemoglobinopathies, recent travel to endemic areas.
Exam: inspect for pallor, jaundice, cyanosis, petechiae, bruising, splenomegaly (palpate left upper quadrant, note size, tenderness).
Exam: auscultate heart for murmurs, gallop, rub; lungs for crackles, wheeze; abdomen for hepatomegaly, ascites (inspection, percussion, shifting dullness).
Exam: check peripheral pulses, capillary refill, skin temperature; assess for clubbing, cyanosis.
Exam: perform a simple bedside test – haemoglobinometer (finger‑stick Hb) to estimate severity; note it cannot replace full haematology panel.
Exam: note that a normal peripheral smear does not exclude early severe malaria; parasitaemia may be low initially.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use a tiered approach, prioritising tests that are available and clinically relevant.
b: Reticulocyte count: <2% indicates hypoproliferative anaemia; >3% suggests haemolysis or bleeding.
Peripheral smear: look for microcytosis, hypochromia, target cells, sickle cells, schistocytes, blasts, parasites; morphology directs differential.
Iron studies: ferritin <15 ng/mL (or <30 ng/mL if inflammation present) and transferrin saturation <15% confirm iron deficiency.
Hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbS >80% = sickle disease; 20‑45% with normal HbF = trait; HbA₂ >3.5% = β‑thalassaemia.
Malaria: thick film for parasitaemia, thin film for species; >5% parasitaemia or any parasitaemia with organ dysfunction = severe malaria.
Coombs test: positive indicates immune haemolysis; negative suggests non‑immune causes.
Bone marrow aspirate: used when blasts >20% or unexplained cytopenias; look for dysplasia, blasts, Auer rods.

sections.p: Classify anaemia and haemolysis using WHO and local guidelines, recognising that thresholds vary by age, pregnancy and comorbidity.
b: Anaemia severity (WHO): <7 g/dL = severe; 7‑9.9 g/dL = moderate; ≥10 g/dL = mild in adults; children and pregnant women have lower cut‑offs.
Haemolysis severity: schistocytes >1% with falling Hb >2 g/dL in 24 h = microangiopathic haemolysis; consider TTP if ADAMTS13 <10% and neurological signs present.
Severe malaria: parasitaemia >5% in non‑immune or any parasitaemia with organ dysfunction (renal failure, jaundice, shock).
Acute leukaemia: blasts ≥20% of nucleated cells on smear; urgent referral for chemotherapy.
Sickle‑cell crisis: pain episode with Hb drop >2 g/dL, chest pain, or organ dysfunction; treat with hydration and analgesia.

sections.p: Differentiate conditions that mimic key smear findings by integrating clinical context and ancillary tests.

t.b: Seen in thalassaemia, liver disease, post‑splenectomy; differentiate by Hb electrophoresis and liver function tests.
Indicative of mechanical hemolysis, DIC, TTP; rule out by coagulation profile, ADAMTS13 activity, and platelet count.
Present in sickle disease, not trait unless hypoxic; confirm with Hb electrophoresis and clinical history of pain crises.
Falciparum shows ring forms, banana‑shaped gametocytes; vivax shows Schuffner stippling; differentiate by species identification on thin film.
Myeloid blasts with Auer rods suggest AML; lymphoid blasts suggest ALL; confirm with flow cytometry and cytogenetics.

sections.p: A systematic ladder ensures rapid stabilisation, targeted therapy based on film findings, and timely escalation in low‑resource settings.
b: 1. Stabilise airway, breathing, circulation; give oxygen if SpO2 < 92 % and ensure adequate IV access.
2. Confirm the dominant film pattern (e.g., severe malaria, hemolysis, leukaemia) with rapid bedside tests before definitive therapy.

3. Initiate disease‑specific treatment: IV artesunate for severe malaria, broad‑spectrum antibiotics for suspected bacterial sepsis with haemolysis, steroids for immune‑mediated hemolysis, or referral for chemotherapy if blasts > 20 %.

4. Provide supportive care: transfuse packed RBCs only if Hb < 7 g/dL (or < 8 g/dL with cardiac stress), give folic acid for haemolysis, maintain hydration, and treat pain aggressively in sickle‑cell crises.
5. Monitor: repeat film after 24‑48 h, track Hb, LDH, bilirubin, renal function, and parasitaemia; watch for rising schistocytes or worsening organ dysfunction.
6. Escalate or refer when: schistocytes > 1 % with ADAMTS13 suspicion, parasitaemia > 5 % with organ failure, blasts > 20 % or rapid Hb fall > 2 g/dL in 24 h, or inability to provide ICU‑level care.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key adverse reactions and interactions that frequently arise when treating common film abnormalities.
b: Artesunate may cause delayed hemolysis; check Hb at day 7 and repeat film; if haemolysis persists, consider transfusion and monitor renal function.
Corticosteroids increase infection risk; give prophylactic antibiotics only if prolonged (> 2 weeks) high‑dose therapy is required.
Blood transfusion can precipitate allo‑immunisation; use leukoreduced, cross‑matched units and document patient’s antibody screen.
Aminoglycosides for severe sepsis are nephrotoxic; monitor serum creatinine daily and avoid if baseline renal failure.
Hydroxyurea for sickle‑cell disease can cause myelosuppression; check full blood count every 4 weeks and hold if neutrophils < 1.5 × 10⁹/L.

sections.p: Recognise life‑threatening sequelae that demand urgent higher‑level care.
b: Acute hemolytic crisis: Hb drop > 2 g/dL in 24 h, rising LDH, and schistocytes > 1 %; start plasma exchange only if TTP is clinically probable and ADAMTS13 testing is pending.
Severe malaria: parasitaemia > 5 % with any organ dysfunction (renal failure, cerebral signs, severe anaemia); give IV artesunate, arrange ICU admission, and monitor glucose.
Leukaemic blast crisis: blasts > 20 % with rising white count; urgent referral to oncology for induction chemotherapy; avoid delay for additional tests if clinical picture is clear.

Sickle‑cell acute chest syndrome: new infiltrate on chest X‑ray, hypoxia, or fever; start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, give oxygen, consider exchange transfusion if SpO2 < 92 % despite supplemental O₂.

sections.p: Conditions that modify film interpretation, laboratory values, or therapeutic choices.
b: HIV may cause cytopenias and opportunistic infections that mimic malaria; order CD4 count and consider CMV or mycobacterial smear if film shows atypical inclusions.
Active TB can cause anaemia of chronic disease; ferritin may be high despite iron deficiency; use soluble transferrin receptor if available.
Malnutrition lowers ferritin and transferrin saturation; interpret iron studies with C‑reactive protein to assess inflammation.
Pregnancy physiologically dilutes Hb; target Hb ≥ 11 g/dL in first/third trimester; avoid teratogenic drugs (e.g., methotrexate) and use ACTs safe in pregnancy for malaria.
Renal failure reduces erythropoietin; film may show normocytic anaemia; give erythropoiesis‑stimulating agents only after dialysis adequacy is confirmed.
Liver disease elevates bilirubin and may cause target cells; avoid hepatotoxic drugs (e.g., high‑dose paracetamol) and monitor LFTs during therapy.

sections.p: Tailored considerations for vulnerable populations in low‑resource environments.
b: Children: use weight‑based dosing for artesunate; monitor for hypoglycaemia after severe malaria; avoid routine transfusion unless Hb < 7 g/dL or symptomatic.
Elderly: lower transfusion threshold (Hb < 7 g/dL) unless cardiac disease; watch for drug‑induced marrow suppression; adjust antihypertensives if fluid overload from aggressive hydration.

People with HIV: screen for drug‑drug interactions between antiretrovirals and antimalarials (e.g., protease inhibitors increase artesunate levels); prophylactic cotrimoxazole may mask bacterial sepsis on film.
Low‑resource settings: if thin film unavailable, use thick film for parasite detection; when automated counters are absent, rely on manual reticulocyte count and clinical severity scores.

facts: Severe anaemia: Hb < 7 g/dL in stable patients; transfuse if symptomatic or <7 g/dL.
Moderate anaemia: Hb 7‑9 g/dL; monitor cardiac stress and consider transfusion if comorbidities.
Iron deficiency ferritin cut‑off: <15 ng/mL (or <30 ng/mL with inflammation).
Transferrin saturation < 15 % supports iron deficiency; > 45 % suggests overload.
Schistocytes > 1 % with falling Hb and thrombocytopenia raise suspicion for TTP; confirm with ADAMTS13 if available.
Severe malaria: parasitaemia >5 % or any parasitaemia with organ dysfunction; treat with IV artesunate.
Auer rods in blasts confirm myeloid lineage; indicates acute myeloid leukaemia.
Howell‑Jolly bodies on film indicate functional asplenia, especially in sickle cell disease.
Target cells suggest thalassaemia or haemoglobinopathies; differentiate by Hb electrophoresis.
Reticulocyte count > 2 % with anaemia points to haemolysis or blood loss; < 2 % suggests production problem.

mnemonics.t: Malaria, Anemia, Leukaemia, Thalassaemia – common causes of abnormal red cell morphology in East Africa.
Red cell size, shape, colour – systematic review of film findings.

vivas.q: What are the three key steps in a bedside examination of a patient with suspected anaemia?
vivas.a: Inspect for pallor, assess for jaundice or scleral icterus, palpate for splenomegaly (soft, non‑tender enlargement suggests haemolysis) and check for peripheral edema.

vivas.q: How do you differentiate iron‑deficiency anaemia from anaemia of chronic disease on a peripheral film and basic labs?
vivas.a: Iron deficiency shows microcytic hypochromic cells, low ferritin (<15 ng/mL) and low transferrin saturation; chronic disease shows normal or high ferritin and low saturation.

vivas.q: Why is plasma exchange not automatically started when schistocytes are seen?
vivas.a: Plasma exchange is reserved for confirmed or strongly suspected TTP, which requires clinical pentad and ADAMTS13 testing; other microangiopathies need different management.

vivas.q: What is the significance of Howell‑Jolly bodies on a smear?
vivas.a: They indicate functional asplenia, common in sickle cell disease and post‑splenectomy, and predispose to encapsulated infections.

vivas.q: When is IV artesunate indicated for malaria?
vivas.a: In severe malaria defined by parasitaemia >5 % (or >2 % in non‑immune) with any organ dysfunction, or any parasitaemia with cerebral involvement.

vivas.q: A 19‑year‑old with fever, sore throat, atypical lymphocytes and positive heterophile test – which cell is the target of EBV?
vivas.a: B‑lymphocytes; EBV infects CD21‑positive B cells causing atypical reactive lymphocytes.

vivas.q: Describe the typical morphology of Plasmodium falciparum gametocytes on a thin film.
vivas.a: Banana‑shaped, elongated with a curved, slender appearance, often occupying a single RBC without enlarging it.

vivas.q: Which stain is preferred for air‑dried blood films and why?
vivas.a: Wright‑Giemsa stain; it provides excellent cytoplasmic detail and differentiates haemoglobinised cells and parasites.

vivas.q: What film finding is characteristic of functional asplenia in children with HbSS?
vivas.a: Howell‑Jolly bodies, target cells and Pappenheimer bodies; spherocytes are not typical.

vivas.q: A dimorphic RBC population suggests which clinical scenario?
vivas.a: Co‑existing iron deficiency and thalassaemia or haemoglobinopathy, or recent transfusion with mixed donor and recipient cells.

vivas.q: Name the cytoplasmic inclusion seen in myeloid blasts and its diagnostic relevance.
vivas.a: Auer rods – needle‑like azurophilic granules confirming acute myeloid leukaemia.

vivas.q: Which physiological process explains hypersegmented neutrophils in B12 deficiency?
vivas.a: Impaired DNA synthesis leads to delayed nuclear maturation while cytoplasmic maturation proceeds, producing hypersegmentation.

vivas.q: How does the presence of Auer rods influence management of acute leukaemia?
vivas.a: It directs therapy toward AML protocols and excludes lymphoid regimens; urgent referral for cytogenetics is needed.

vivas.q: Outline the thin versus thick film utility in malaria diagnosis.
vivas.a: Thin film identifies species and parasite stage; thick film increases sensitivity for low parasitaemia. If thin unavailable, rely on thick for detection, then confirm with rapid test.

vivas.q: Summarise a systematic approach to anaemia using the peripheral film.
vivas.a: History → diet, bleeding, infections; exam → pallor, splenomegaly; retic count; MCV; film morphology; targeted labs (iron, B12, folate, haemolysis screen).

vivas.q: What are the key bone‑marrow findings in Myelodysplastic Syndromes?
vivas.a: Dyspoietic erythroid, granulocytic and megakaryocytic lineages with ring sideroblasts, increased blasts (<20 %), and cytogenetic abnormalities.

mcqs.q: A child from a malaria‑endemic area presents with fever, pallor and a peripheral smear showing 6 % parasitized RBCs. What is the next best step?
o: Observe and repeat smear in 24 h
mcqs.e: Parasitaemia >5 % qualifies as severe malaria; IV artesunate is first‑line.

mcqs.q: Which of the following film findings most strongly suggests a diagnosis of acute myeloid leukaemia?
mcqs.e: Auer rods are pathognomonic for myeloid blasts.

mcqs.q: A patient with sickle cell disease presents with acute chest pain, falling Hb and schistocytes 2 %. Which condition must be ruled out before plasma exchange?
mcqs.e: TTP requires plasma exchange; other causes need different treatment.

mcqs.q: In a pregnant woman (second trimester) with microcytic hypochromic anaemia, which ferritin cut‑off is appropriate to diagnose iron deficiency?
mcqs.e: Ferritin <30 ng/mL is recommended in pregnancy due to inflammatory changes.

mcqs.q: Which stain is most suitable for an air‑dried peripheral smear to visualise parasites and cytoplasm?
mcqs.e: Wright‑Giemsa provides excellent cytoplasmic detail for parasites.

mcqs.q: A 60‑year‑old with macrocytosis, hypersegmented neutrophils and low B12 is evaluated. Which physiological process is impaired?
mcqs.e: B12 deficiency hampers DNA synthesis, causing nuclear‑cytoplasmic asynchrony.

mcqs.q: Which peripheral smear finding indicates functional asplenia?
mcqs.e: Howell‑Jolly bodies persist when the spleen cannot remove nuclear remnants.

mcqs.q: A dimorphic red cell population is most likely seen in which scenario?
mcqs.e: Both iron deficiency and thalassaemia or recent transfusion can produce two distinct cell sizes.

cases.v: A 28‑year‑old woman, HIV‑positive, presents with fever, jaundice and dark urine. Hb 6.5 g/dL, retic 5 %. Smear shows numerous schistocytes (2 %), no parasites, and occasional spherocytes. Platelets 80 ×10⁹/L.

qs.q: What urgent condition must be considered?
qs.a: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) – microangiopathic haemolysis with thrombocytopenia.

qs.q: Which bedside test helps assess severity before labs return?
qs.a: Neurological exam for confusion or seizures; renal assessment for oliguria.

qs.q: If ADAMTS13 testing is unavailable, what is the immediate management?
qs.a: Start plasma exchange urgently while arranging transfer; give steroids as adjunct.

mistakes: Assuming any palpable spleen in children is normal; any enlargement warrants investigation.
Using Hb <8 g/dL as a universal transfusion trigger; stable patients often tolerate Hb 7 g/dL.
Starting plasma exchange solely on schistocytes >1 % without clinical TTP criteria.
Confusing spherocytes with functional asplenia; the latter shows Howell‑Jolly bodies.
Relying on ferritin <12 ng/mL for iron deficiency; the correct cut‑off is <15 ng/mL (or <30 ng/mL with inflammation).
Expecting sickle cells on a routine smear in sickle‑cell trait; they appear only under hypoxia or special tests.
Treating malaria with oral artemisinin alone when parasitaemia exceeds 5 %; IV artesunate is required.
